nameStory: This microscopic algae is named after Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg, a 19th-century German naturalist who pioneered the study of tiny organisms. The genus name Pleurotaenium comes from Greek words meaning 'side-band,' referring to the distinctive ridged patterns that run along the sides of these elegant single-celled creatures.
description: Pleurotaenium ehrenbergii is a microscopic single-celled algae that belongs to a group called desmids - beautifully symmetrical organisms that live in freshwater. Each cell is elongated and cylindrical, typically measuring about 200-400 micrometers long (roughly the width of a few human hairs). These tiny green gems are only visible under a microscope, where they appear as delicate, translucent rods with intricate surface patterns. Despite being just one cell, they're considered among the most elegant and geometrically perfect organisms in nature.

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Long, narrow cylindrical cells that are slightly tapered at both ends, resembling a tiny green hot dog when viewed under the microscope

idTips.label: Surface ridges
idTips.description: Distinctive longitudinal ridges or bands running lengthwise along the cell wall, creating a ribbed texture like a tiny corduroy fabric

idTips.label: Cell ends
idTips.description: Rounded or slightly flattened end caps that may appear darker or more opaque than the rest of the cell

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green color from chloroplasts arranged in ribbon-like bands inside the cell

idTips.label: Cell division
idTips.description: Often found in pairs after cell division, with the two halves still connected end-to-end like tiny train cars

habitat: Found in clean, soft-water ponds, bogs, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in acidic waters with low mineral content. These microscopic organisms thrive in quiet backwaters among aquatic plants and in the shallow edges of pristine mountain lakes and kettle ponds.

seasonality.spring: Most active during spring warming when they begin rapid reproduction. Best collected from shallow, sun-warmed areas of ponds and streams.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance in warm summer months. Can be found floating freely in the water column or clinging to submerged vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less active as temperatures cool. Often concentrate in protected coves and shallow areas that retain warmth.
seasonality.winter: Survive as resistant stages in bottom sediments. Rarely found actively swimming during cold months.

funFact: Each individual cell of Pleurotaenium ehrenbergii is perfectly symmetrical - if you drew a line through its middle, both halves would be mirror images, making these single-celled organisms living examples of mathematical perfection that would make any geometry teacher proud!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other elongated desmids like Closterium, but Pleurotaenium species have straight sides rather than the curved, crescent shape of Closterium. Memory trick: Pleurotaenium stays 'straight as a ruler' while Closterium curves like a 'crescent moon.'
contextualKnowledge: These organisms are actually considered 'indicator species' - their presence suggests very clean, unpolluted water. Scientists use desmids like Pleurotaenium to assess the health of freshwater ecosystems, as they're among the first to disappear when water quality declines.
compareHints: Pleurotaenium ehrenbergii differs from its relatives by being relatively smooth with subtle ridges, while P. nodosum has prominent swellings or nodes along its length. P. coronatum has distinctive crown-like ornaments at the cell ends, and P. trabecula shows more pronounced cross-banding patterns.
